questions.q:
Match each figure in Column I with the figure congruent to it in Column II.

Part (b): halves the diameter to 7.5 cm and says not congruent

questions.q: (a) Is a rectangle 9 cm by 4 cm congruent to one that is 4 cm by 9 cm? What must be done to the second before superimposing? (b) Is it congruent to a rectangle 9 cm by 5 cm? Why?
questions.a: (a) Yes; rotate it (a quarter turn) so the 9 cm sides lie together. (b) No; the breadths 4 cm and 5 cm differ, so it cannot fit exactly.
s: Part (a): yes, after rotating so the 9 cm sides match
Part (b): no, because the breadths differ

questions.q: Priya traces a scalene arrow on tracing paper. She has to turn the paper over before it fits exactly on a second arrow, so she says: 'The arrows are not congruent, because I had to flip mine.' True or False? Give the reason.
questions.a: False. Flipping (as well as rotating) is allowed while superimposing, so an arrow that fits exactly after being flipped is congruent to the other.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: flipping is allowed, so exact fit means congruent

questions.q: Tile T1 is a rectangle 30 cm by 20 cm. Tile T2 fits exactly over T1 only after a quarter turn. Tile T3 fits exactly over T2 only after a half turn. Naveen says T3 and T1 need not be congruent because he never placed them together. (a) Is he right? Give the reason. (b) State T3's two measurements.
questions.a: (a) No. T2 is congruent to T1 and T3 is congruent to T2, so T3 has the same shape and size as T1 (turning, sliding or flipping never changes shape or size). (b) 30 cm by 20 cm.
s: Part (a): No, with the chain T3 to T2 to T1 as the reason
Part (b): 30 cm by 20 cm

questions.q: A cafe owner has a coaster of radius 4.2 cm. A second coaster is measured across its widest part as 8.5 cm. (a) Are the two coasters congruent? Give the reason. (b) By how much would the second coaster's diameter have to change to make them congruent?
questions.a: (a) No. The first has diameter 2 x 4.2 = 8.4 cm, but the second has 8.5 cm, so their radii differ (4.2 cm and 4.25 cm) and they cannot fit exactly. (b) It would have to be 0.1 cm smaller (8.4 cm).
s: Part (a): No, comparing 8.4 cm with 8.5 cm (or the radii)
Part (b): 0.1 cm smaller

questions.q:
Mr Rao's class tested four pairs of figures and recorded each verdict. Pair 1: rectangles 120 cm by 45 cm and 45 cm by 120 cm; Asha measured the sides and wrote 'congruent'. Pair 2: circles of diameter 18 cm and radius 9 cm; Bilal wrote 'congruent'. Pair 3: two leaf cutouts, each 14 cm long and 6 cm across at the widest; Chetan wrote 'congruent, since the measurements match'. Pair 4: rectangles 8 cm by 5 cm and 8 cm by 5.5 cm; Dina measured only the longer sides, found both 8 cm, and wrote 'not congruent'.
(a) Which two verdicts are justified by the method used? (b) Dina's verdict happens to be right, but her method does not support it. What should she have measured? (c) Why can Chetan's measurements not settle his pair, and what should he do? (d) Mr Rao has time to re-check only one of the four verdicts by tracing and superimposing. Which should he choose? Give the reason.
questions.a: (a) Asha's (the sides 120 and 45 match in both) and Bilal's (diameter 18 cm means radius 9 cm, equal radii). (b) The shorter sides as well: 5 cm and 5.5 cm differ, which proves the rectangles are not congruent; the equal longer sides prove nothing. (c) A leaf has no short list of lengths that fixes it; two matching measurements leave many different leaf shapes, so he must trace one leaf and place it over the other. (d) Pair 3: it is the only one that cannot be settled by measuring at all, while Dina's pair needs just one more measurement.
s: Part (a): Asha's and Bilal's verdicts
Part (b): measure the shorter sides, 5 cm against 5.5 cm
Part (c): lengths do not fix a leaf; trace and superimpose
Part (d): re-check pair 3, with the reason

questions.a: (a) CA = 26 - 7 - 9 = 10 cm. (b) All three sides match (7, 9, 10), so SSS holds. AB = 7 cm matches ZX, BC = 9 cm matches XY and CA = 10 cm matches YZ, so A goes with Z, B with X, C with Y: ΔABC ≅ ΔZXY.

Part (b): SSS with the order ΔABC ≅ ΔZXY

questions.a: (a) P goes with Y, Q with Z and R with X, and A goes with P, B with Q, C with R. So A goes with Y, B with Z and C with X: ΔABC ≅ ΔYZX. (b) BC matches ZX (B with Z, C with X), so ZX = 11 cm.
s: Part (a): ΔABC ≅ ΔYZX, found by chaining the two matchings
Part (b): ZX = 11 cm

s: Verdict: Dev's statement is wrong
Shows AB (9 cm) would fall on CB (5 cm)
Gives the correct matching ΔABD ≅ ΔCDB

Writes ΔABC ≅ ΔYXZ

Part (b): ΔABC ≅ ΔADC

Part (d): yes, corresponding angles are equal

(c) Write a correct congruence starting with ΔABC, and name the condition. (d) Write another correct statement that starts with ΔCAB. (e) Which angle of ΔABC equals ∠Q?
questions.a: (a) A is matched with Q and B with R, so AB is matched with QR = 7 cm, but AB = 5 cm; the statement is wrong. (b) AB = 5 cm matches RP = 5 cm, BC = 6 cm matches PQ = 6 cm, and CA = 7 cm matches QR = 7 cm. (c) A with R, B with P, C with Q: ΔABC ≅ ΔRPQ, by SSS. (d) C, A, B correspond to Q, R, P: ΔCAB ≅ ΔQRP. (e) ∠Q corresponds to C, so ∠Q = ∠C.
s: Part (a): AB matched with QR = 7 cm, so the statement is wrong
Part (b): the three matching side pairs
Part (c): ΔABC ≅ ΔRPQ, SSS
Part (d): ΔCAB ≅ ΔQRP
Part (e): ∠Q = ∠C

questions.q:
Ms Sharma's school makes triangular flags for Independence Day, which is 4 days away. The template ΔPQR has PQ = 30 cm, QR = 40 cm and RP = 50 cm. Tailor A has made 50 flags with these sides. Tailor B has made 45 flags ΔLMN with LM = 40 cm, MN = 50 cm and NL = 30 cm. Tailor C has made 25 flags with sides 30 cm, 40 cm and 55 cm. The school pays ₹8 for each flag congruent to the template and needs 120 flags.
(a) Which tailors' flags are congruent to the template? (b) Write ΔLMN's congruence with the template in order. (c) How much is paid so far, and how many flags are still short? (d) The 25 missing flags can come from Tailor A, who charges ₹8 each and needs 3 days, or from Tailor B, who charges ₹8 each plus ₹100 for express work and needs 2 days. Decide whom to ask.
questions.a: (a) A and B (SSS); C has 55 cm, not 50 cm. (b) L is between 40 and 30, which meet at Q; M between 40 and 50, at R; N between 50 and 30, at P. So ΔPQR ≅ ΔNLM. (c) 95 x 8 = ₹760; 120 - 95 = 25 short. (d) Tailor A: 25 x 8 = ₹200, ready in 3 days, which is within the 4 days. Tailor B: 200 + 100 = ₹300, ready in 2 days. Both are in time and the flags are congruent either way, so ask Tailor A: the extra day is free and saves ₹100.
s: Part (a): A and B, with C failing on the 55 cm side
Part (b): ΔPQR ≅ ΔNLM
Part (c): ₹760 and 25 short
Part (d): Tailor A at ₹200, ready in 3 days, ₹100 cheaper than Tailor B

questions.q:
Sunil, a carpenter in Ludhiana, makes door panels from rectangular sheets ABCD with AB = 90 cm and BC = 210 cm, each cut along the diagonal BD into two triangular panels. A contractor needs 36 identical triangular panels. Sheets cost ₹400 each, and ready-cut triangular panels cost ₹210 each. Sunil's helper suggests cutting along both diagonals, which cross at O with OA = OB = OC = OD, because each sheet would then give four triangles and 9 sheets would do.
(a) Write CD and DA, and say which condition shows ΔABD ≅ ΔCDB. (b) Is ΔOAB ≅ ΔOBC? Give the reason using sides. (c) Can the helper's 9 sheets supply 36 identical panels? (d) Decide which plan the contractor should follow and what it costs: the helper's, 18 sheets cut along one diagonal, or 36 ready-cut panels.
questions.a: (a) CD = 90 cm and DA = 210 cm; ΔABD ≅ ΔCDB by SSS (AB = CD, AD = CB, BD common). (b) No. ΔOAB has sides OA, OB and AB = 90 cm; ΔOBC has OB, OC and BC = 210 cm. The first two pairs are equal but the third sides, 90 cm and 210 cm, differ, so SSS fails. (c) No. Only opposite triangles are congruent, so 9 sheets give 18 triangles of one kind and 18 of another, not 36 identical ones. (d) Follow neither the helper's plan nor the ready-cut panels: 18 sheets cut along one diagonal give 36 congruent panels for 18 x 400 = ₹7,200, which is ₹360 less than 36 x 210 = ₹7,560.
s: Part (a): CD = 90 cm, DA = 210 cm, SSS
Part (b): No, third sides 90 cm and 210 cm differ
Part (c): No, only 18 of each kind
Part (d): 18 sheets cut along one diagonal, ₹7,200 against ₹7,560

questions.q:
In each row of Column I, ΔABC and ΔPQR have the equal parts shown. Match the row with the conclusion in Column II.
Column I: 1. AB = PQ = 6 cm, BC = QR = 8 cm, ∠B = 100°, ∠Q = 100°  2. AB = PQ = 8 cm, BC = QR = 7 cm, ∠A = ∠P = 50°  3. ∠A = ∠P = 50°, ∠B = ∠Q = 60°, ∠C = ∠R = 70°  4. ABC has sides 6, 8, 7 cm and PQR has PQ = 7, QR = 6, RP = 8 cm
Column II: a. Congruent by SSS  b. Congruent by SAS  c. Same shape only, congruence not guaranteed  d. SSA, congruence not guaranteed
O is the midpoint of PS and also of QR. (a) Name the three equal parts of ΔPOQ and ΔSOR. (b) Write the congruence in order and say which side equals PQ.
questions.a: (a) PO = SO, QO = RO and ∠POQ = ∠SOR (vertically opposite angles). (b) ΔPOQ ≅ ΔSOR by SAS, so PQ = SR.
s: Part (a): PO = SO, QO = RO, vertically opposite angles
Part (b): ΔPOQ ≅ ΔSOR by SAS, PQ = SR

questions.q: Gauri says: 'Two triangles with equal sides of 8 cm and 6 cm and an equal angle of 35° are always congruent.' Is she right?
questions.a: Not always. If the 35° lies between the 8 cm and 6 cm sides, SAS makes them congruent. If it does not, it is the SSA case, where two different triangles may be possible, so she cannot be sure.
s: Verdict: not always
Congruent when the angle is included (SAS)
Not guaranteed when the angle is not included (SSA)

questions.q: ABCD is a rectangle with AB = 12 cm and BC = 5 cm. (a) Name the two sides and the included angle that show ΔABC ≅ ΔCDA by SAS. (b) What is the length of DA, and which angle of ΔCDA equals ∠BAC?
questions.a: (a) AB = CD (12 cm), BC = DA (5 cm) and the included angles ∠B = ∠D = 90°. (b) DA = 5 cm, and ∠BAC = ∠DCA, since A matches C in ΔABC ≅ ΔCDA.
s: Part (a): AB = CD, BC = DA and the right angles at B and D
Part (b): DA = 5 cm and ∠DCA, from the order of the congruence

questions.q: ΔPQR has PQ = 8 cm, PR = 6.5 cm and ∠P = 62°. ΔLMN has LM = 8 cm, LN = 6.5 cm and ∠L = 62°. (a) Are they congruent? Name the condition and write the congruence. (b) QR is measured as 7.4 cm. What is MN, and why?
questions.a: (a) Yes, SAS (the 62° lies between the equal sides): ΔPQR ≅ ΔLMN. (b) MN = 7.4 cm, since QR and MN are corresponding sides.
s: Part (a): SAS and ΔPQR ≅ ΔLMN
Part (b): MN = 7.4 cm as corresponding sides

questions.q: ΔABC ≅ ΔPQR by SAS, with AB = PQ = 7 cm, BC = QR = 9 cm and the included angles ∠B = ∠Q = 64°. Also ∠A = 52°. (a) Find ∠R. (b) Rani writes 'so ∠P = 64°, as the angle given in ΔPQR is 64°'. Find her slip and give the correct value of ∠P.
questions.a: (a) ∠C = 180° - 64° - 52° = 64°, and C corresponds to R, so ∠R = 64°. (b) She matched P with B. The equal 64° angles are ∠B and ∠Q, since B corresponds to Q. P corresponds to A, so ∠P = ∠A = 52°.
s: Part (b): P corresponds to A, so ∠P = 52°

questions.q: ΔABC has AB = 7 cm, BC = 6 cm, ∠B = 47°; ΔXYZ has XY = 7 cm, YZ = 6 cm, ∠Y = 47°. (a) Are they congruent? Name the condition. (b) If the 47° were ∠A and ∠X instead (same sides), could you still be sure?
questions.a: (a) Yes, SAS, ΔABC ≅ ΔXYZ, the angle being between the two sides. (b) No. The angle is then not included, which is the SSA case, and two different triangles can fit.
s: Part (a): congruent by SAS with the angle between the sides
Part (b): not sure, since it becomes SSA

questions.q: Show that equal angles alone cannot make two triangles congruent: describe two triangles with angles 50°, 60° and 70°.
questions.a: Draw one with a 5 cm side between the 50° and 60° angles, and another with a 10 cm side between the same angles. Both have angles 50°, 60°, 70°, but their sizes differ, so they are not congruent.
s: Both triangles have the same three angles
Gives different side lengths such as 5 cm and 10 cm
Concludes same shape but not congruent

questions.q: In ΔABC, AB = 7 cm, AC = 9 cm, ∠A = 65°. Write the three measurements for ΔXYZ that make ΔABC ≅ ΔXYZ by SAS, and name the matching vertices.
questions.a: XY = 7 cm, XZ = 9 cm, ∠X = 65°. A matches X, B matches Y, C matches Z.
s: Gives XY = 7 cm and XZ = 9 cm
Gives ∠X = 65° between them
States the matching A-X, B-Y, C-Z

questions.q:
A workshop owner compares four pairs of triangular plates, ΔABC and ΔPQR. Pair 1: AB = PQ = 7 cm, AC = PR = 9 cm, ∠A = ∠P = 48°. Pair 2: AB = PQ = 9 cm, AC = PR = 7 cm, ∠B = ∠Q = 48°. Pair 3: ∠A = ∠P = 48°, ∠B = ∠Q = 62°, ∠C = ∠R = 70°, and no side is measured. Pair 4: AB = QR = 7 cm, BC = PQ = 9 cm, ∠B = ∠Q = 48°.
(a) Is Pair 1 certainly congruent? Name the condition. (b) Pair 2 has the same two lengths but the 48° is at B and Q, opposite the 7 cm side. What goes wrong? (c) What can be said about Pair 3? (d) Is Pair 4 certainly congruent? If so write the congruence in order. (e) Which single extra equality would make Pair 3 certainly congruent, and by which condition?
questions.a: (a) Yes, SAS: the 48° lies between the 7 cm and 9 cm sides in both. (b) The 48° is not between the two given sides, so this is the SSA case. The 7 cm side opposite the 48° is shorter than AB = 9 cm but longer than 9 sin 48° (about 6.7 cm), so two different triangles can fit and congruence is not certain. (c) The plates have the same shape but may differ in size, so congruence is not certain. (d) Yes, SAS: ∠B lies between AB and BC, and ∠Q between PQ and QR; AB matches QR and BC matches PQ, so ΔABC ≅ ΔRQP. (e) Any one pair of corresponding sides, for example AB = PQ, gives ASA (or AAS), because all three angles are already equal.
s: Part (a): yes, SAS
Part (b): the angle is not included, SSA, so not certain
Part (c): same shape only, not certain
Part (d): SAS with ΔABC ≅ ΔRQP
Part (e): one pair of corresponding sides, giving ASA or AAS

questions.q: Compare two constructions. In (i) PQ = 9 cm, PR = 7 cm and ∠P = 40°. In (ii) PQ = 9 cm, QR = 7 cm and ∠P = 40°. (a) In which is the angle included? (b) Which condition applies to it? (c) For the other, why can two triangles be drawn? (d) Which one lets Rabia be sure of congruence?
questions.a: (a) (i): ∠P is between PQ and PR. (b) SAS. (c) In (ii) the 40° is not between the sides (SSA), and an arc of 7 cm from Q cuts the line from P at two points. (d) Construction (i), because SAS guarantees congruence.
s: Part (a): (i) has the included angle
Part (b): SAS
Part (c): arc cuts the line at two points in SSA
Part (d): (i) is certain

questions.q:
The fete committee cuts triangular rangoli sheets to match a template with two sides of 24 cm and 18 cm and 50° between them, and pays ₹5 for each sheet congruent to it. Four students cut sheets. Anil cuts 12 sheets with sides 24 cm and 18 cm and 50° between. Bela cuts 10 with 24 cm and 18 cm and 70° between. Chitra cuts 8 with sides 18 cm and 24 cm and 50° between. Dev cuts 6 with sides 24 cm and 20 cm and 50° between. The rangoli is laid on Friday at 4 pm and needs 30 matching sheets.
(a) Which students' sheets are congruent to the template? (b) For each of the others, say which part fails the SAS condition. (c) How much is paid? (d) The 10 missing sheets can be cut by Anil at ₹5 each, who will finish by Friday noon, or supplied exactly to the template by Dev on Wednesday at ₹7 each. Decide whom to ask.
questions.a: (a) Anil and Chitra, by SAS. (b) Bela's included angle is 70°, not 50°; Dev's second side is 20 cm, not 18 cm. (c) (12 + 8) x 5 = ₹100. (d) Ask Anil. Anil's would cost 10 x 5 = ₹50 and arrive by Friday noon; Dev's cost 10 x 7 = ₹70. Both are in time and both sets are congruent to the template (SAS), so ask Anil: ₹20 cheaper.
s: Part (a): Anil and Chitra
Part (b): Bela's angle 70°, Dev's side 20 cm
Part (c): ₹100
Part (d): Anil, ₹50 against ₹70, both in time and both congruent

questions.q:
A gardener marks triangular flower beds with ropes. Bed 1 has sides 12 m and 9 m with 40° between them. Bed 2 has sides 9 m and 12 m with 40° between them. Bed 3 has sides 12 m and 9 m with 55° between them. Five beds are needed: three like bed 1 and two like bed 3. A stone-edging mould made for one shape can be reused for every congruent bed. The mould for bed 1 costs ₹2,400 and the mould for bed 3 costs ₹5,000. Re-marking a bed to a different angle between the 12 m and 9 m sides costs ₹800 per bed. The 55° angle is not essential to the design.
(a) Is bed 2 congruent to bed 1? Give the condition. (b) Is bed 3 congruent to bed 1? Give the reason. (c) What do the moulds cost if the five beds are made as planned? (d) Compare three plans: as planned; re-mark the two beds of 55° to 40°; re-mark the three beds of 40° to 55°. Which is cheapest?
questions.a: (a) Yes, SAS: the same two sides with the same angle between them. (b) No, the angle between the 12 m and 9 m sides is 55°, not 40°. (c) 2,400 + 5,000 = ₹7,400. (d) As planned: ₹7,400. Re-mark the two to 40°: one mould, 2,400 + 2 x 800 = ₹4,000. Re-mark the three to 55°: 5,000 + 3 x 800 = ₹7,400. Re-marking the two beds to 40° is cheapest, saving ₹3,400.
s: Part (a): yes, SAS
Part (b): no, 55° against 40°
Part (d): ₹4,000 by re-marking the two beds to 40°

questions.q: Surveyor Reena has ΔABC with ∠B = 45°, ∠C = 75° and BC = 40 m. A second plot ΔPQR has ∠Q = 45°, ∠P = 60° and QR = 40 m. What can she conclude?
questions.a: Congruent: ∠R works out to 75° and QR lies between ∠Q and ∠R
o: Congruent: ∠R works out to 75° and QR lies between ∠Q and ∠R
Not congruent, because ∠C = 75° but the plot gives no 75° angle
Cannot say, because the equal side is not between the two angles
Congruent, because one angle and one side are equal in both plots

o: RHS, since each brace has a right angle and a 4 m side to compare
AAS: two angles and the 4 m side, which is opposite the 35° angle in both braces
ASA, since the 4 m side lies between the two given angles in each brace
Not enough: the hypotenuse of each brace has not been measured

questions.a: Congruent: the third angles are 70°, so ASA applies
o: Congruent: the third angles are 70°, so ASA applies
Not sure: the 8 cm side is not between the angles
Congruent by SSA

questions.a: Not congruent: corresponding sides AC and DF differ
o: Not congruent: corresponding sides AC and DF differ
Congruent by AAS, as two angles and a side are equal
Congruent, since all three angles are equal
Not congruent, since the side must lie between the angles

questions.q:
Read the statements about ASA and AAS.
Statement 1: ASA and AAS are the same condition, because the equal side always lies between the equal angles.
Statement 2: In AAS the third angle is found by adding the two given angles.
Statement 3: Two triangles with two equal angles and the equal side between them are congruent.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: 3 only
o: 3 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only

questions.q: Isha says: 'If two angles and a side not between them in one triangle equal the matching parts of another (AAS), the triangles are still congruent.' Do you agree?
questions.a: Yes. The third angle is 180° minus the two given angles, so it is equal in both triangles. The equal side now lies between two equal angles, so ASA applies and the triangles are congruent.
s: Verdict: agree
Finds the third angle as 180° minus the other two
Shows ASA now applies

questions.q:
For each pair of triangles ΔABC and ΔPQR in Column I, match the statement in Column II that settles congruence.
Column I: 1. ∠A = ∠P = 48°, ∠B = ∠Q = 57°, AB = PQ = 9 cm  2. ∠A = ∠P = 48°, ∠B = ∠Q = 57°, BC = QR = 9 cm  3. ΔABC has ∠A = 48°, ∠B = 57°, AB = 9 cm and ΔPQR has ∠P = 48°, ∠R = 75°, PQ = 9 cm  4. ∠A = ∠P = 48°, ∠B = ∠Q = 57°, ∠C = ∠R = 75°
Column II: a. ASA: the equal side lies between two given equal angles  b. AAS: the equal side is not between the two given angles, in both triangles  c. ASA, but only after the third angle of one triangle is found  d. Congruence not guaranteed
In ΔABC, ∠A = 48°, ∠C = 62° and BC = 6 cm. In ΔXYZ, ∠X = 48°, ∠Z = 62° and YZ = 6 cm. (a) Find ∠B and ∠Y. (b) Name the condition for ΔABC ≅ ΔXYZ and write it in order.
questions.a: (a) ∠B = 180° - 110° = 70° and ∠Y = 70°. (b) AAS (BC lies opposite ∠A, not between the given angles), or ASA once the third angles are found: ΔABC ≅ ΔXYZ.
s: Part (a): ∠B = ∠Y = 70°
Part (b): names AAS (or ASA after the third angle) and writes ΔABC ≅ ΔXYZ

questions.q: In ΔABC, AD is perpendicular to BC and AD bisects ∠BAC. (a) Which condition gives ΔABD ≅ ΔACD, and which parts are equal? (b) What follows for AB and AC, and for BD and DC?
questions.a: (a) ASA: ∠BAD = ∠CAD, the common side AD, and ∠ADB = ∠ADC = 90°. (b) AB = AC and BD = DC, as corresponding sides.
s: Part (a): ASA with ∠BAD = ∠CAD, AD common, ∠ADB = ∠ADC
Part (b): AB = AC and BD = DC

questions.q: Two straight rods AD and BC cross at O, with AB ∥ CD and BO = CO. (a) Name the angle pairs that are equal in ΔAOB and ΔDOC, and the reason for each. (b) Name one condition that shows ΔAOB ≅ ΔDOC. What follows for AB and DC?
questions.a: (a) ∠OAB = ∠ODC, as alternate angles (AB ∥ CD, transversal AD), and ∠AOB = ∠DOC, as vertically opposite angles. (b) AAS: the equal side BO = CO is opposite ∠OAB and ∠ODC. (ASA also works, since ∠OBA = ∠OCD as alternate angles with transversal BC, and BO lies between ∠OBA and ∠AOB.) Hence ΔAOB ≅ ΔDOC and AB = DC.
s: Part (a): alternate angles and vertically opposite angles
Part (b): a valid condition (AAS, or ASA with the third angle pair), so AB = DC

questions.q: In ΔABC, ∠A = 72°, ∠B = 33° and AC = 8 cm. In ΔPQR, ∠P = 72°, ∠R = 75° and PQ = 8 cm. (a) Find ∠C and ∠Q. (b) Can Sonal conclude that ΔABC ≅ ΔPQR? Compare where the 8 cm side lies in each triangle.
questions.a: (a) ∠C = 180° - 72° - 33° = 75° and ∠Q = 180° - 72° - 75° = 33°. (b) No. The 8 cm side AC lies between ∠A = 72° and ∠C = 75°. The 8 cm side PQ lies between ∠P = 72° and ∠Q = 33°. They are not corresponding sides, so ASA and AAS do not apply; the triangles have the same angles, so the same shape, but congruence is not shown.
s: Part (a): ∠C = 75° and ∠Q = 33°
Part (b): No, since AC and PQ are in different positions and do not correspond

questions.q: ΔABC has ∠A = 35°, ∠B = 85° and BC = 11 cm. ΔDEF has ∠D = 35°, ∠F = 60° and EF = 11 cm. Sam says: 'The two triangles are congruent.' True or False? Give the reason.
questions.a: True. ∠C = 180° - 35° - 85° = 60° = ∠F and ∠E = 180° - 35° - 60° = 85° = ∠B. BC and EF are both opposite the 35° angle, so the triangles are congruent by AAS (ΔABC ≅ ΔDEF).
s: Verdict: True, after finding the third angles 60° and 85°
Reason: BC and EF are the sides opposite the equal 35° angles, so AAS applies

Assertion (A): In ΔABC and ΔDEF, if ∠B = ∠E = 40°, ∠C = ∠F = 75° and AB = DE, the triangles are congruent.
Reason (R): The third angles ∠A and ∠D are both 65°, so AB lies between two known equal angles in each triangle.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: Two triangles have angles 40°, 60° and 80°, and each has a side of 5 cm. Show that they still need not be congruent.
questions.a: In one triangle the 5 cm side can be opposite the 40° angle; in the other it can be opposite the 80° angle. The sides are not in corresponding positions, so the sizes differ and the triangles are not congruent.
s: Both have the same angles and a 5 cm side
Places the 5 cm side opposite different angles
Concludes the side must correspond

questions.q: For ΔABC with ∠A = 50°, AB = 6 cm and ∠B = 70°, write the data for ΔPQR that is congruent by ASA, and then different data for ΔXYZ that is congruent by AAS.
questions.a: ΔPQR: ∠P = 50°, PQ = 6 cm, ∠Q = 70° (ASA). For AAS, first find ∠C = 180° - 120° = 60°. ΔXYZ: ∠X = 50°, ∠Z = 60° and XY = 6 cm; XY is opposite ∠Z and not between the angles, so AAS gives ΔABC ≅ ΔXYZ.
s: ASA data with the included side 6 cm
AAS data with ∠C = 60° found
Places the 6 cm side opposite ∠Z

questions.q: Rina's triangle T1 has ∠B = 40°, BC = 7 cm and ∠C = 65°. Triangle T2 has ∠D = 75°, ∠E = 40° and EF = 7 cm. Triangle T3 has ∠K = 40°, ∠L = 65° and KM = 7 cm. (a) Find ∠A in T1. (b) Is T2 congruent to T1? Give the condition and write the congruence. (c) Is T3 congruent to T1? Explain using the position of the 7 cm side. (d) Change one measurement of T3 so that it becomes congruent to T1.
questions.a: (a) ∠A = 180° - 105° = 75°. (b) In T2, ∠F = 180° - 115° = 65°, so EF lies between 40° and 65° as BC does in T1: ASA (AAS as given), ΔABC ≅ ΔDEF. (c) No. In T3 the 7 cm side KM lies between ∠K = 40° and ∠M = 75°, not between 40° and 65°, so it does not correspond to BC. (d) Make the side KL (between ∠K = 40° and ∠L = 65°) 7 cm; then ASA gives T3 ≅ T1.
s: Part (a): 75°
Part (b): third angle 65°, ASA/AAS, ΔABC ≅ ΔDEF
Part (c): not congruent because the 7 cm side is in a different position
Part (d): sets KL = 7 cm, giving ASA

questions.q: Triangle ABC has AB = AC and ∠A = 40°. BD is drawn perpendicular to AC with D on AC, and CE is drawn perpendicular to AB with E on AB. (a) Find ∠ABC and ∠ACB, and say why they are equal. (b) Name the equal angles and the common side of ΔBDC and ΔCEB, and the condition. (c) Write the congruence in order and say what it shows about BD and CE. (d) Find ∠DBC and ∠ECB.
questions.a: (a) ∠ABC = ∠ACB, because AB = AC (angles opposite equal sides are equal), and each is (180° - 40°)/2 = 70°. (b) ∠BDC = ∠CEB = 90°, ∠DCB = ∠ACB = 70° = ∠ABC = ∠EBC, and BC is common (opposite the right angle in both): AAS. (c) ΔBDC ≅ ΔCEB (B with C, D with E, C with B), so BD = CE. (d) ∠DBC = 180° - 90° - 70° = 20°, and ∠ECB = ∠DBC = 20° as corresponding angles.
s: Part (a): 70° each, with the isosceles reason
Part (b): the equal angles, the common side BC, and AAS
Part (c): ΔBDC ≅ ΔCEB, so BD = CE
Part (d): ∠DBC = ∠ECB = 20°

questions.q:
For two sheds, roof frame 1 has ∠A = 50°, ∠B = 60° and AB = 3 m. Frame 2 has ∠P = 50°, ∠Q = 60° and PQ = 3 m. Frame 3 has ∠X = 50°, ∠Y = 60° and YZ = 3 m. The sheds need 8 frames congruent to frame 1. The contractor has 6 frames like frames 1 or 2 and 5 frames like frame 3. Option A: make 2 new frames at ₹2,500 each. Option B: hire 2 frames like frame 1 from a neighbouring school at ₹1,200 per frame per month. The sheds are needed for 3 months.
(a) Find the third angle of frame 1. (b) Are frames 1 and 2 congruent? Name the condition. (c) Are frames 1 and 3 congruent? Explain using where the 3 m side lies. (d) Which option is cheaper over the 3 months? Decide.
questions.a: (a) 70°. (b) Yes, ASA: AB lies between ∠A and ∠B, and PQ between ∠P and ∠Q. (c) No: in frame 3 the 3 m side YZ lies opposite ∠X, not between the 50° and 60° angles, so it does not correspond to AB; the five frames of type 3 cannot be used. (d) Two new frames cost 2 x 2,500 = ₹5,000. Hiring costs 2 x 1,200 x 3 = ₹7,200. Make the new frames; hiring looks cheaper per frame but is ₹2,200 dearer over 3 months.
s: Part (a): 70°
Part (b): yes, ASA
Part (c): no, the 3 m side is opposite ∠X, not between the angles
Part (d): make new frames, ₹5,000 against ₹7,200

questions.q:
Surveyor Tara checks whether triangular plots are congruent. Plot 1 has ∠A = 48°, ∠C = 62° and BC = 40 m. For Plot 2 she measures ∠P = 48°, ∠Q = 70°, ∠R = 62° and QR = 40 m. For Plot 4 she measures ∠K = 62°, ∠L = 70° and KM = 40 m. Measuring an angle costs ₹600 and measuring a side costs ₹400. Plot 3 is ΔXYZ, to be compared with Plot 1, whose angles and all three sides are already known. For Plot 3 she must choose between measuring two angles and one side, or all three sides, but a pond blocks side ZX and a boat to measure it costs ₹700 extra.
(a) Find ∠B of Plot 1. (b) Are Plots 1 and 2 congruent? Name the condition. (c) Do Plot 4's measurements show that it is congruent to Plot 1? Compare where the 40 m side lies. (d) Which plan should she use for Plot 3? Decide.
questions.a: (a) ∠B = 180° - 48° - 62° = 70°. (b) Yes, AAS: ∠A = ∠P, ∠B = ∠Q and BC = QR (the side opposite ∠A and ∠P). (c) No. In Plot 4, ∠M = 180° - 62° - 70° = 48°, and KM is opposite ∠L = 70°. In Plot 1, BC is opposite ∠A = 48°. The 40 m sides do not correspond. (d) Two angles and a side cost 2 x 600 + 400 = ₹1,600; three sides cost 3 x 400 + 700 = ₹1,900. Use two angles and a side, ₹300 cheaper.
s: Part (a): 70°
Part (b): yes, AAS
Part (c): no, the 40 m sides lie opposite 70° and 48°
Part (d): two angles and a side, ₹1,600 against ₹1,900

questions.q: A kite-shaped frame ABCD has ∠ABC = ∠ADC = 90° and AB = AD. The diagonal AC is drawn. Which statement gives ΔABC ≅ ΔADC?
o: RHS: right angles at B and D, common hypotenuse AC, and AB = AD
SAS: AB = AD, AC common, and the angle that lies between those sides
SSS: all three sides of each triangle are known from the data given
ASA: the two right angles with the common side AC lying between them
questions.a: RHS: right angles at B and D, common hypotenuse AC, and AB = AD

questions.q: Brace ABC has its right angle at B, with BC = 24 cm and AC = 40 cm. Brace DEF has its right angle at E, with DE = 24 cm and DF = 40 cm. A carpenter says they can be interchanged. Which congruence statement is justified?
questions.a: ΔABC ≅ ΔFED by RHS
o: ΔABC ≅ ΔFED by RHS
ΔABC ≅ ΔDEF by RHS
ΔABC ≅ ΔFED by SSA, which may fail
ΔABC ≅ ΔDEF by SAS

questions.q: In ΔABC, ∠B = 90°, AC = 13 cm and AB = 5 cm. In ΔPQR, ∠Q = 90°, PR = 13 cm and PQ = 6 cm. Ria says RHS shows ΔABC ≅ ΔPQR. (a) Is she right? Give the reason. (b) Which single measurement of ΔPQR would make her claim correct, and what would the congruence be?
questions.a: (a) No. RHS needs the right angle, the hypotenuse and one other side to be equal in both, but the sides AB and PQ are 5 cm and 6 cm, so RHS is not satisfied and congruence cannot be claimed. (b) PQ = 5 cm. Then the hypotenuses AC and PR match, AB matches PQ, and ΔABC ≅ ΔPQR (A with P, B with Q, C with R).
s: Part (a): No, because AB = 5 cm and PQ = 6 cm are not equal
Part (b): PQ = 5 cm, giving ΔABC ≅ ΔPQR

questions.q: In ΔABC, ∠B = 90°, AB = 8 cm and BC = 15 cm. In ΔDEF, ∠E = 90°, DE = 8 cm and EF = 15 cm. Tara says the triangles are congruent by RHS. Uma says by SAS. (a) Who is right? Give the reason. (b) Write the congruence in order.
questions.a: (a) Uma. RHS needs the hypotenuse and a side, but 8 cm and 15 cm are the sides that form the right angle, not the hypotenuse. SAS applies: AB = DE, BC = EF and the included angles ∠B = ∠E = 90°. (b) ΔABC ≅ ΔDEF.
s: Part (a): Uma, because 8 cm and 15 cm are not hypotenuse sides but enclose the 90° angle (SAS)
Part (b): ΔABC ≅ ΔDEF

questions.q: A vertical pole TF stands on level ground. Two wires TA and TB, each 13 m long, run from its top T to ground points A and B on opposite sides of the foot F. (a) Show that ΔTFA ≅ ΔTFB by RHS, listing the three equal parts. (b) FA is measured as 5 m. What is FB, and what does this say about F?
questions.a: (a) ∠TFA = ∠TFB = 90°, the hypotenuses TA = TB = 13 m, and TF is common. (b) FB = FA = 5 m (corresponding sides), so the foot F is the midpoint of AB.
s: Part (a): right angles at F, equal wires, common TF, so RHS
Part (b): FB = 5 m and F is the midpoint of AB

questions.q: Kabir says: 'Two right-angled triangles, each with one side of 8 cm and one side of 10 cm, are always congruent by RHS.' True or False? Give the reason or the correction.
questions.a: False. RHS needs the equal sides to be the hypotenuse and one other side. Here the 10 cm side could be the hypotenuse in one triangle and a side beside the right angle in the other, so congruence is not guaranteed.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: RHS needs the 10 cm side to be the hypotenuse in both triangles

questions.q: Right triangles ΔABC (right angle at B) and ΔPQR (right angle at Q) have AC = PR = 13 cm and BC = PQ = 5 cm. If AB = 12 cm, then QR = ___ cm.
ABCD is a rectangle. (a) Use RHS to show that ΔABC ≅ ΔCDA by listing the three equal parts. (b) Name the angle of ΔCDA that equals ∠BAC.

Part (b): ∠DCA

questions.q: ΔABC has ∠B = 90°, AB = 6 cm, BC = 8 cm. ΔXYZ has ∠Y = 90°, XY = 6 cm, YZ = 10 cm. Show that a right angle and one equal side are not enough for congruence.
questions.a: Both have a right angle and a 6 cm side, but their other sides are 8 cm and 10 cm, so one cannot be fitted over the other. A right angle and one side alone do not fix the triangle; the hypotenuse (or another side) must also match.

questions.q: Write measurements for right triangles ΔPQR (right angle at P) and ΔXYZ (right angle at Y) so that RHS proves them congruent. Write the congruence in order.
questions.a: Example: ΔPQR with ∠P = 90°, PQ = 5 cm and hypotenuse QR = 13 cm; ΔXYZ with ∠Y = 90°, XY = 5 cm and hypotenuse XZ = 13 cm. The hypotenuses QR and XZ match, and PQ matches YX, so P goes with Y, Q with X, R with Z: ΔPQR ≅ ΔYXZ.
s: Gives right angles, equal hypotenuses and one equal side
Identifies hypotenuses QR and XZ
Writes the congruence in matching order

questions.q: Neha writes: 'ΔABC has ∠B = 90°, AB = 7 cm and AC = 25 cm. ΔDEF has ∠E = 90°, DE = 7 cm and DF = 25 cm. Step 1: AC and DF are the hypotenuses. Step 2: AB = DE and AC = DF. Step 3: By RHS, ΔABC ≅ ΔDEF. Step 4: Therefore BC = DE.' (a) Which step is wrong? (b) What does BC equal, and why? (c) Suppose it turns out that ∠E is not known. What is left of Steps 1 to 3, and is congruence guaranteed? (d) Explain why A must correspond to D and C to F.
questions.a: (a) Step 4. (b) BC = EF, because B corresponds to E and C to F, so BC and EF are corresponding sides; DE corresponds to AB. (c) Only AB = DE and AC = DF remain, with no angle equal, so RHS is lost and two pairs of sides are not enough: congruence is not guaranteed. (d) The right angles at B and E correspond, so the hypotenuses opposite them, AC and DF, correspond; AB = DE then matches A with D, and so C goes with F.
s: Part (a): Step 4
Part (b): BC = EF, with the correspondence B-E, C-F
Part (c): only two pairs of sides remain, not guaranteed
Part (d): right angles correspond, hypotenuses correspond, so A-D and C-F

questions.q: Two sets of data are given for ΔABC. Data I: AB = 12 cm, AC = 8 cm and ∠B = 25°. Data II: AB = 12 cm, AC = 13 cm and ∠B = 90°. (a) Is the angle included between the two given sides in either data set? (b) How many different triangles fit Data I, and why? (c) How many non-congruent triangles fit Data II, and why? (d) What feature of Data II makes the difference?
questions.a: (a) No. In both the angle is at B, but the second given side is AC, so the angle is not between the two given sides. (b) Two. Draw AB = 12 cm and a line from B at 25°; the arc of 8 cm from A cuts the line at two points, giving two triangles of different shape. (c) One. The arc of 13 cm from A cuts the perpendicular at B and its extension at two points that are mirror images of each other in AB, so the triangles are congruent. (d) The right angle: it makes the second intersection point a mirror copy, which is why RHS guarantees congruence while the general SSA does not.
s: Part (a): no, the angle is not included in either
Part (b): two triangles, the arc cuts the line twice
Part (c): one triangle up to congruence, mirror images
Part (d): the right angle gives the mirror copy, so RHS works

questions.q:
At a school fair, tent A has a vertical pole of 3 m and a rope of 5 m running from its top to a stake on level ground. The stake is found to be 4 m from the foot of the pole. Each tent has 4 such ropes. Tent B is built with a 3 m pole and 5 m ropes, and rope costs ₹40 per metre.
(a) In the triangle of pole, rope and ground for tent A, which side is the hypotenuse and where is the right angle? (b) If tent B's pole is vertical, how far is each of its stakes from the foot of the pole, and which condition tells you? (c) What do the ropes of tents A and B together cost? (d) At tent B an inspector measures a stake 4.3 m from the foot of the pole, with the pole 3 m and the rope 5 m. What does this show about the pole, and should the inspector accept the set-up?
questions.a: (a) The rope is the hypotenuse; the right angle is where the pole meets the ground. (b) 4 m, by RHS: with a right angle, a 5 m hypotenuse and a 3 m side, the triangle is congruent to tent A's. (c) 2 x 4 x 5 x 40 = ₹1,600. (d) If the pole were vertical, RHS would force the stake to 4 m. At 4.3 m the triangle is not congruent to tent A's, so the pole is not at 90° to the ground; the inspector should not accept it and the pole must be set upright and re-measured.
s: Part (a): the rope; right angle at the foot of the pole
Part (b): 4 m, by RHS
Part (d): the pole is leaning, reject and re-set it

questions.q:
A shop orders 20 triangular boards congruent to board P (∠B = 90°, BC = 12 cm, AC = 15 cm), paying ₹150 for each. Twelve boards arrive with ∠Y = 90°, YZ = 12 cm and XZ = 15 cm. The supplier also offers eight more boards with sides of 12 cm and 15 cm, whose angles are unknown, at ₹90 each; the shop must pay for all eight even if they do not fit. The shop may instead have each of the eight measured for ₹60 per board and pay only for those found with the right angle opposite the 15 cm side (so that 15 cm is the hypotenuse). In the supplier's last batch of eight, six were not right-angled.
(a) Which of the twelve are congruent to P, and by which condition? (b) Why can the eight not yet be called congruent to P? (c) What is the payment for the twelve? (d) If the next batch behaves like the last (two boards with the right angle opposite the 15 cm side), compare the two ways of buying the eight. Decide.
questions.a: (a) All twelve, by RHS (right angle, hypotenuse 15 cm, side 12 cm). (b) Their angles are unknown, so the data are only two sides. A board whose right angle lies between the 12 cm and 15 cm sides has a longer hypotenuse, so it would not fit P; congruence is not guaranteed. (c) 12 x 150 = ₹1,800. (d) Paying for all eight unseen: 8 x 90 = ₹720 for two usable boards. Measuring first: 8 x 60 + 2 x 90 = ₹660. Measure first: it costs ₹60 less if the batch repeats.
s: Part (a): all twelve, by RHS
Part (b): only two sides known, no right angle
Part (d): measure first, ₹660 against ₹720

s: Verdict: agrees with Mira

Case of 40° as the apex angle: 40°, 70°, 70°

questions.q: One angle of an isosceles triangle is 80°. (a) Find the other two angles in each possible case. (b) Show that if the given angle is 100° there is only one case.
questions.a: (a) If 80° is one of the two equal angles, the angles are 80°, 80° and 20°. If 80° is the odd angle, the other two are equal and (180° - 80°)/2 = 50° each, giving 80°, 50°, 50°. (b) Two equal angles of 100° would add to 200°, more than 180°, so 100° must be the odd angle and the others are (180° - 100°)/2 = 40° each.

Part (b): RHS, so BD = DC and D is the midpoint

Part (b): forms a = (180 - a)/2 and solves to 60°

Part (b): 112° is the sum of the base angles, to be subtracted from 180°

ΔABD ≅ ΔACD by AAA, since the two triangles look alike in the figure

questions.q: Show that a triangle with AB = AC cannot have ∠B = 90°.
questions.a: Since AB = AC, ∠B = ∠C. If ∠B = 90° then ∠C = 90°, and ∠B + ∠C = 180° already, leaving nothing for ∠A. The angles of a triangle must add up to 180° with ∠A greater than 0, so it cannot exist.
s: Uses ∠B = ∠C
Concludes no angle is left for ∠A

Chooses ∠A = 30° or an equivalent
Solves with (180° - a)/2 = 75°

questions.q: ΔPQR is isosceles with PQ = PR and ∠P = 56°. PS is drawn perpendicular to QR. (a) Name the condition that gives ΔPSQ ≅ ΔPSR and the three equal parts. (b) What does this say about ∠Q and ∠R? (c) Find ∠Q and ∠R. (d) Find ∠QPS and check the angles of ΔPSQ add up to 180°.
questions.a: (a) RHS: PQ = PR, ∠PSQ = ∠PSR = 90° and PS common. (b) ∠Q = ∠R. (c) ∠Q = ∠R = (180° - 56°)/2 = 62°. (d) ∠QPS = 28° (corresponding to ∠RPS, half of 56°), and 28° + 62° + 90° = 180°.
s: Part (a): RHS with three equal parts
Part (b): ∠Q = ∠R
Part (c): 62° each
Part (d): 28° and the check to 180°

questions.q: Two isosceles triangles stand on the same base BC, on opposite sides of it. In ΔABC, AB = AC and ∠BAC = 50°. In ΔDBC, DB = DC and ∠BDC = 110°. The line AD is drawn. (a) Find ∠ABC. (b) Find ∠DBC. (c) Find ∠ABD. (d) Show that ΔABD ≅ ΔACD, and hence find ∠BAD and ∠ADB, checking that the angles of ΔABD add up to 180°.
questions.a: (a) ∠ABC = (180° - 50°)/2 = 65°. (b) ∠DBC = (180° - 110°)/2 = 35°. (c) ∠ABD = 65° + 35° = 100°. (d) AB = AC, DB = DC and AD is common, so ΔABD ≅ ΔACD by SSS. Then ∠BAD = ∠CAD = 25° (half of 50°) and ∠ADB = ∠ADC = 55° (half of 110°). Check: 25° + 100° + 55° = 180°.
s: Part (a): 65°
Part (b): 35°
Part (c): 100°
Part (d): SSS, ∠BAD = 25°, ∠ADB = 55°, with the check

questions.q:
An engineer's clerk lists four roof trusses, each an isosceles triangle with two equal rafters. The rule is that each base angle must be at least 60°. The committee takes the cheapest truss that meets the rule. The clerk's table shows: Truss A, apex 64°, base angle 62°, ₹36,000. Truss B, apex 50°, base angle 65°, ₹40,000. Truss C, apex 30°, base angle 55°, ₹42,000. Truss D, apex 100°, base angle 40°, ₹28,000. The budget is ₹45,000.
(a) Find the true base angle of each truss from its apex angle and say which two entries in the clerk's table are wrong. (b) Which trusses meet the rule? (c) What is the largest apex angle for which the rule is met, and what kind of triangle has it? (d) Which truss should the committee choose, and which truss would the clerk's table have led them to choose?
questions.a: (a) Base angles: A (180° - 64°)/2 = 58°, B 65°, C 75°, D 40°. The entries for A (62° listed) and C (55° listed) are wrong. (b) B (65°) and C (75°) meet the rule. (c) Base angle at least 60° means (180° - apex)/2 is at least 60°, so the apex is at most 60°; at exactly 60° all three angles are 60°, an equilateral triangle. (d) The cheapest that meets the rule is B at ₹40,000, within the budget. The clerk's table would have led to A at ₹36,000, which has a base angle of only 58°.
s: Part (a): 58°, 65°, 75°, 40°, with the entries for A and C wrong
Part (b): trusses B and C
Part (c): apex at most 60°, equilateral
Part (d): truss B, not A

questions.q:
A rangoli group makes flower patterns from paper equilateral triangles of side 15 cm. Each flower has triangles meeting at one centre point and filling the full turn of 360°. They need 18 flowers. Readymade triangles cost ₹4 each. One sheet costing ₹25 can be cut into 8 such triangles, but cutting one sheet takes 20 minutes and the students have 240 minutes in all.
(a) What is the angle of each triangle at the centre? (b) How many triangles meet at the centre of one flower? (c) How many triangles are needed in all, and what do readymade ones cost for all of them? (d) Find the cheapest plan that can be finished in the time: how many sheets are cut, how many readymade triangles are bought, and what is the total cost?
questions.a: (a) 60°. (b) 360° / 60° = 6. (c) 18 x 6 = 108 triangles; 108 x 4 = ₹432. (d) In 240 minutes they can cut 240 / 20 = 12 sheets, giving 96 triangles for 12 x 25 = ₹300. They then buy the other 108 - 96 = 12 readymade triangles for 12 x 4 = ₹48. Total ₹348, which is ₹84 less than buying all 108.
s: Part (a): 60°
Part (b): 6 triangles at one centre
Part (c): 108 triangles, ₹432 if all are bought
Part (d): 12 sheets cut (96 triangles) plus 12 bought, ₹348

Part (b): AD = CB

questions.q: PQRS is a rectangle with the diagonal QS drawn. (a) Using only the equal sides of the rectangle and the common side, which condition shows ΔPQS ≅ ΔRSQ? (b) Which angle equals ∠PSQ, and why?
questions.a: (a) SSS: PQ = RS and PS = RQ (opposite sides of a rectangle) and QS is common to both. (b) ∠RQS, since P corresponds to R, Q to S and S to Q, so ∠PSQ and ∠RQS are corresponding angles.
s: Part (a): SSS with PQ = RS, PS = RQ and QS common
Part (b): ∠RQS, as corresponding angles

questions.q: AB bisects ∠CAD, and AC = AD. (a) Which condition shows ΔCAB ≅ ΔDAB? (b) What follows for BC and BD?
questions.a: (a) SAS: AC = AD, ∠CAB = ∠DAB (the included angle) and AB common. (b) BC = BD.
s: Part (a): SAS with common AB
Part (b): BC = BD

questions.q: In ΔABC, AB = AC and D is the midpoint of BC, so ΔABD ≅ ΔACD by SSS. If ∠BAD = 28°, then ∠BAC = ___ degrees.
ΔETN ≅ ΔARY, with ET = 7.5 cm, TN = 9 cm and ∠T = 52°. (a) Find AR, RY and ∠R. (b) Is ΔNET ≅ ΔYAR a correct way to write the same congruence? Say why.
questions.a: (a) AR = 7.5 cm, RY = 9 cm and ∠R = 52°. (b) Yes: N, E, T match Y, A, R in the same order, as E-A, T-R and N-Y did originally.
s: Part (a): AR = 7.5 cm, RY = 9 cm, ∠R = 52°
Part (b): yes, since N, E, T keep matching Y, A, R in order

questions.q: In ΔABC, AB = AC, and D is a point on BC with AD perpendicular to BC and BD = DC = 9 cm. (a) Which condition uses the right angle, and which parts are equal? (b) Which condition uses BD = DC and the right angle between BD and AD? (c) Which condition uses only sides? (d) Which of the three conditions would still work if the right angle were not stated, and why?
questions.a: (a) RHS: hypotenuses AB = AC, ∠ADB = ∠ADC = 90° and side AD common. (b) SAS: BD = DC, ∠ADB = ∠ADC and AD common. (c) SSS: AB = AC, BD = DC and AD common. (d) Only SSS: it uses AB = AC, BD = DC and the common side AD, and no angle, while RHS and SAS both need the right angle.
s: Part (a): RHS
Part (b): SAS
Part (c): SSS
Part (d): SSS only, since the other two need the right angle

questions.q: PQ is common to ΔPQR and ΔPQS, with ∠PQR = ∠PQS and PR = PS. Show that ΔPQR ≅ ΔPQS cannot be concluded from this.
questions.a: The equal parts are the common side PQ, the angle at Q, and the sides PR = PS. The equal angle ∠PQR = ∠PQS is not between PQ and PR, so this is the SSA case. SSA does not guarantee congruence, so the triangles may differ.
s: Lists the equal parts
Notes the angle is not included, so SSA
Concludes SSA does not guarantee congruence

questions.q: Write a short question about ΔPQR and ΔSTU, giving ∠Q = ∠T, QR = TU and ∠R = ∠U, whose answer is PQ = ST. Include the reasoning that answers it.
questions.a: Question: In ΔPQR and ΔSTU, ∠Q = ∠T, QR = TU and ∠R = ∠U. Show that PQ = ST. Answer: QR lies between ∠Q and ∠R, and TU between ∠T and ∠U, so ΔPQR ≅ ΔSTU by ASA. PQ and ST are corresponding sides, so PQ = ST.
s: Gives a question with the three equal parts
Names ASA with the included side QR = TU
Concludes PQ = ST as corresponding sides

questions.q: Karan says: 'If two triangles share a common side and have one more pair of equal sides, they are congruent.' Is he right? Test with ΔABC and ΔABD where AB = 5 cm, AC = AD = 6 cm, BC = 4 cm and BD = 7 cm.
questions.a: No. AB is common and AC = AD, but BC = 4 cm and BD = 7 cm differ, so the triangles are not congruent. A third equal pair (or an included angle) is needed.
s: Verdict: Karan is wrong
Shows BC = 4 and BD = 7 are unequal
Says a third pair is needed

questions.q: ABCD has AB ∥ DC and AB = DC, and the diagonal BD is drawn. (a) Which pair of angles is equal, and why? (b) Which condition shows ΔABD ≅ ΔCDB, and what is the common side? (c) Write the congruence in order. (d) AB is 7.5 cm and AD is 4.2 cm. Find DC and BC, and state which angle of ΔCDB equals ∠A.
questions.a: (a) ∠ABD = ∠CDB, as alternate angles (AB ∥ DC, transversal BD). (b) SAS: AB = CD, the angle between AB and BD equals the angle between CD and DB, and BD is the common side. (c) ΔABD ≅ ΔCDB (A with C, B with D, D with B). (d) DC = AB = 7.5 cm and BC = AD = 4.2 cm; ∠A = ∠C.
s: Part (a): alternate angles ∠ABD = ∠CDB
Part (b): SAS with BD common
Part (c): ΔABD ≅ ΔCDB
Part (d): DC = 7.5 cm, BC = 4.2 cm, ∠A = ∠C

questions.q:
Imran builds a kite ABCD with AB = AD = 35 cm and CB = CD = 50 cm. The spine AC and the cross-stick BD cross at O. The cross-stick is a 56 cm rod.
(a) Show ΔABC ≅ ΔADC and name the condition. (b) What does this tell you about ∠BAC and ∠DAC? (c) Show ΔABO ≅ ΔADO and deduce BO and DO. (d) Imran marks the crossing point at 35 cm from B on the rod, 'so that the kite flies higher'. Is this consistent with the kite he has drawn? Decide and justify with (c).
questions.a: (a) AB = AD, CB = CD and AC is common: SSS, so ΔABC ≅ ΔADC. (b) ∠BAC = ∠DAC, as corresponding angles. (c) AB = AD, ∠BAO = ∠DAO and AO is common: SAS, so ΔABO ≅ ΔADO and BO = DO. (d) No. BO = DO means the spine crosses the rod at its midpoint, 28 cm from B. Marking it at 35 cm would make BO ≠ DO, contradicting the kite he has drawn, so he must move the mark to 28 cm.
s: Part (a): SSS
Part (b): ∠BAC = ∠DAC
Part (c): SAS, BO = DO
Part (d): reject 35 cm; the crossing must be at the midpoint, 28 cm

questions.q:
Meera wants the width of a river without crossing it. A tree P stands on the far bank. She stands at Q on her bank so that PQ is at right angles to the bank. She walks along the bank 40 m to R, then 40 m further to S, turns at right angles away from the river and walks until the flag at R and the tree P are in line, at point T. She finds ST = 65 m.
(a) Name the three equal parts of ΔPQR and ΔTSR. (b) Write the congruence and name the condition. (c) What is PQ? (d) The council will build a bridge only if the river is under 70 m wide. Meera then finds that her turn at S was 84°, not 90°. Can the council rely on the 65 m figure? Decide.
questions.a: (a) QR = SR = 40 m, ∠Q = ∠S = 90°, ∠PRQ = ∠TRS (vertically opposite). (b) ΔPQR ≅ ΔTSR by ASA. (c) PQ = TS = 65 m. (d) No. With ∠S = 84° the angle at S no longer equals ∠Q = 90°, so ASA fails and the triangles are not shown congruent; ST need not equal PQ. The council should not approve on 65 m. Meera must redo the turn at 90° and measure ST again.
s: Part (a): QR = SR, the two right angles, the vertically opposite angles
Part (b): ΔPQR ≅ ΔTSR by ASA
Part (c): PQ = 65 m
Part (d): ASA fails with 84°, so do not rely on 65 m; redo it at 90°
